questions.prompt: In the paired demonstrations, what distinguishes longitudinal motion from transverse motion, and what can remain comparable?
questions.answer: Longitudinal displacement runs along the spring or chain, while transverse displacement runs across its length. The demonstration tunes the restoring effects so that the two directions can share the same oscillation rate, despite the different directions of visible motion.
rubric: The answer distinguishes motion along the system from motion across it.
The answer explains that comparable restoring conditions can produce matching rates without making the motion directions identical.

questions.prompt: Why can two coupled masses have a same-direction mode and an opposite-direction mode?
questions.answer: Coupling allows coordinated patterns in which both masses oscillate at one shared rate with a stable relationship. In one mode they move together, while in the other they move in opposite directions. The different patterns involve different restoring effects and therefore different mode frequencies.
rubric: The answer describes same-direction and opposite-direction coordinated patterns.
The answer connects a normal mode to a shared rate and stable movement relationship.

questions.prompt: A two-mass system is moving as the sum of two normal modes. Why is it misleading to assign the mixed motion just one normal-mode frequency?
questions.answer: Each component mode retains its own frequency. Adding them produces a combined motion containing both rates, so the mixture is not itself one of the single-frequency normal modes.
rubric: The answer preserves the distinct frequencies of the component modes.
The answer distinguishes a sum of modes from a single normal mode.

questions.prompt: The middle mass stays still in one three-mass mode while the outer masses move. Does that mean the middle mass is broken or absent?
questions.answer: No. In that coordinated mode, the middle position is a node of displacement. The same mass can move in other modes because the pattern of coordinated motion changes.
rubric: The answer identifies a node as a location of zero displacement in a particular mode.
The answer explains that being motionless in one mode does not imply being motionless in all modes.

questions.prompt: A six-mass chain has six normal modes. Does that establish that their frequencies are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 times its lowest frequency?
questions.answer: No. The number of modes and the spacing of their frequencies are different properties. The finite-chain demonstration has one mode per mass, but its frequencies are generally not integer multiples of the lowest one.
rubric: The answer distinguishes mode count from frequency ratios.
The answer explicitly avoids imposing the ideal-string harmonic series on a finite chain.

questions.prompt: Why does the membrane animation’s use of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz not prove that every membrane naturally has a harmonic series?
questions.answer: Those frequencies were assigned to the illustrated membrane motions for teaching. The source notes distinguish them from the rectangular membrane’s natural mode frequencies, so the chosen spacing is a feature of this demonstration rather than a universal membrane result.
rubric: The answer identifies the frequencies as illustrative assigned values.
The answer distinguishes the demonstration from a general claim about natural membrane frequencies.

questions.prompt: How could you test the lecture’s prediction of equally spaced peaks in a vocal-fold vibration spectrum?
questions.answer: Record an appropriate laryngeal vibration signal and inspect its spectrum. Compare the peak frequencies to ask whether the gaps are approximately equal, as predicted for the illustrated harmonic source. The test compares a measurement with a prediction, rather than treating a schematic membrane animation as the measurement.
rubric: The answer identifies a vibration measurement and a spectral peak-spacing comparison.
The answer distinguishes a theoretical or schematic prediction from an observed result.

questions.prompt: Two coupled masses can move together in one mode and in opposite directions in another. Why can those patterns have different frequencies even though the masses are unchanged?

options.text: The coordinated patterns deform the coupling elements differently, so the effective restoring action differs between the modes of the same system.
options.feedback: A mode concerns a coordinated spatial pattern as well as a rate. Changing the relationship between the mass motions changes the restoring interactions without requiring different physical masses.

options.text: The opposite-direction pattern has a higher rate because it contains more moving mass than the same-direction pattern, even though the two physical masses are unchanged.
options.feedback: The mass count has not changed. The patterns differ in how the coupling deforms.

options.text: The apparent rate difference is a phase difference, so the two panels have the same frequency and differ in the timing of their turning points.
options.feedback: The source gives distinct mode frequencies. Phase and frequency are different quantities.

options.text: The rate difference reflects damping in the slower pattern, with the spatial relationship between the masses having no restoring effect of its own.
options.feedback: The displayed model is undamped. Its coordinated patterns involve different restoring interactions.

questions.answer: A mode concerns a coordinated spatial pattern as well as a rate. Changing the relationship between the mass motions changes the restoring interactions without requiring different physical masses.
rubric: Recognize different coordinated patterns in the same physical system.
Connect differing deformation patterns to different restoring action and frequency.

questions.prompt: A six-mass row has six modes, and an ideal fixed–fixed string diagram shows integer harmonics. Which conclusion respects the different system assumptions?

options.text: The six-mass row has integer frequency ratios because its six independent patterns can be numbered 1 through 6 in increasing order.
options.feedback: Mode labels count patterns; they do not establish integer frequency ratios.

options.text: The fixed endpoints make the six-mass row equivalent to a continuous string for frequency spacing, despite its finite number of moving masses.
options.feedback: Shared endpoints do not remove the distinction between finite discrete and continuous systems.

options.text: The ideal string’s integer sequence implies an equal frequency gap in the finite row as well, with the difference between the systems confined to how their amplitudes are drawn.
options.feedback: Their frequency relationships differ, not just their display amplitudes.

options.text: The six-mass row has one mode per moving mass in the displayed direction, but its frequency ratios do not have to match the ideal continuous string’s integer sequence.
options.feedback: Mode count does not establish harmonic spacing. The source explicitly distinguishes finite discrete-chain ratios from the integer harmonics of an ideal continuous fixed–fixed string.

questions.answer: Mode count does not establish harmonic spacing. The source explicitly distinguishes finite discrete-chain ratios from the integer harmonics of an ideal continuous fixed–fixed string.
rubric: Separate mode count from frequency ratios.
Retain the distinction between finite discrete and ideal continuous systems.

questions.prompt: The bottom row sums the two displayed normal modes. Which description best distinguishes the mixture from either individual mode?

options.text: The mixture has a single frequency equal to the average of the two component rates, because adding displacements also averages their frequencies.
options.feedback: Adding displacement functions does not replace their frequencies with their numerical average.

options.text: The mixture has the faster mode’s frequency, because the slower component increases the amplitude of that mode rather than contributing a separate rate.
options.feedback: The slower component remains a distinct frequency contribution in the sum.

options.text: The mixture has the slower mode’s frequency, because cancellation of some displacements removes the faster rate from the combined motion.
options.feedback: Partial displacement cancellation does not generally remove the faster component from the whole mixture.

options.text: The mixture contains both component frequencies, so its total motion is not a single normal mode with one shared mode frequency.
options.feedback: Superposition adds the mode motions. It does not erase their separate frequencies or require every mass to follow one of the individual coordinated patterns alone.

questions.answer: Superposition adds the mode motions. It does not erase their separate frequencies or require every mass to follow one of the individual coordinated patterns alone.
rubric: Explain the sum as containing both mode contributions.
Distinguish several component rates from a single normal-mode rate.

questions.prompt: In one three-mass mode, the middle mass remains at its resting position while the outer masses move oppositely. What does that observation establish?

options.text: The middle mass is mechanically disconnected for that pattern, so the remaining outer motion should be analyzed as a system with one fewer mass.
options.feedback: A mode node does not remove the mass or its connections from the system.

options.text: The middle location is a displacement node for that mode, while the same mass can move in other modes of the system.
options.feedback: A node belongs to a particular mode shape. The middle mass’s stillness in that pattern does not imply that it is absent, disconnected, or motionless in every possible motion.

options.text: The middle location is a displacement antinode, where the local movement is smallest despite the large movement in the outer masses.
options.feedback: The displacement terms are reversed. A node has zero displacement in the mode.

options.text: The middle location remains a node in the combined motion, because its zero displacement in this mode carries over when other modes are added.
options.feedback: Other modes can move that mass. A node of one component is not automatically a node of the mixture.

questions.answer: A node belongs to a particular mode shape. The middle mass’s stillness in that pattern does not imply that it is absent, disconnected, or motionless in every possible motion.
rubric: Identify zero displacement as a node in the specified mode.
Avoid generalizing one mode’s node to every motion of the mass.

questions.prompt: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations both display a 100 Hz fundamental. A student concludes that freeing one end never changes the fundamental. Which reply best evaluates that claim?

options.text: The common 100 Hz label establishes that length and wave speed were held fixed, so the boundary change has been tested as the single manipulated condition.
options.feedback: The source specifies separate tuning rather than a single-variable boundary manipulation.

options.text: The common 100 Hz label follows from the fixed endpoint alone, with the free endpoint changing amplitude but leaving the allowed wavelengths unchanged.
options.feedback: The two endpoint conditions change the allowed mode patterns and wavelengths.

options.text: The free-end example should have twice the fixed–fixed fundamental at unchanged length and wave speed, so matching 100 Hz indicates an error rather than retuning.
options.feedback: The fixed–free fundamental is half under those unchanged conditions, and the examples are explicitly retuned.

options.text: The examples were separately tuned, so their matching fundamentals do not isolate a boundary change at fixed length and wave speed.
options.feedback: The source notes specify separate tuning. For the same length and wave speed, the ideal fixed–free fundamental would be half the fixed–fixed one, so equal displayed fundamentals require another condition to differ.

questions.answer: The source notes specify separate tuning. For the same length and wave speed, the ideal fixed–free fundamental would be half the fixed–fixed one, so equal displayed fundamentals require another condition to differ.
rubric: Recognize that matched displayed fundamentals come from separate tuning.
Keep the fixed-length, fixed-wave-speed boundary comparison distinct.

questions.prompt: You want to test the lecture’s prediction of regular harmonic spacing in a laryngeal vibration signal. Which plan directly compares a measurement with that prediction?

options.text: Record one strong spectral peak and use its amplitude to infer the gaps between the remaining frequencies without locating the other peaks.
options.feedback: One peak’s amplitude does not determine spacing between several peak frequencies.

options.text: Record the signal’s total loudness over time and compare its average level with the equal heights assigned to the schematic membrane peaks.
options.feedback: Overall loudness does not directly test spectral frequency spacing.

options.text: Record the relevant vibration signal, examine its spectrum, and compare the frequency gaps between peaks against the predicted regular spacing.
options.feedback: The prediction concerns spectral peak spacing in a measured signal. The supplied lecture proposes the experiment, but it does not supply completed participant data or establish a measured outcome for this page.

options.text: Use the assigned membrane animation as the measured signal, comparing its equally spaced labels with the prediction before describing the result as participant evidence.
options.feedback: The schematic’s assigned frequencies are not a participant measurement of laryngeal vibration.

questions.answer: The prediction concerns spectral peak spacing in a measured signal. The supplied lecture proposes the experiment, but it does not supply completed participant data or establish a measured outcome for this page.
rubric: Measure the relevant vibration signal and spectral peak frequencies.
Distinguish testing a prediction from asserting an unprovided experimental result.

questions.prompt: The reference, larger-mass, and stiffer-spring rows start side by side. Explain how their relative cycle counts over the same viewing interval separate inertia from restoring action.
questions.answer: The reference uses m and K. Increasing mass to 4m with K fixed slows the motion to half the reference rate because the same restoring action changes a heavier mass’s motion more slowly. Increasing effective stiffness to 4K with m fixed doubles the reference rate because the return toward equilibrium is stronger. Comparing cycles over the same interval distinguishes the rate changes from different displacement sizes.
rubric: Hold stiffness fixed when interpreting the larger-mass row and mass fixed when interpreting the stiffer row.
Explain half-rate versus twice-rate through inertia and restoring action, rather than the drawing’s size.

questions.prompt: A student replaces the transverse spring segments with axially stiffer ones but leaves their tension and geometry unchanged. Why is this a different manipulation from increasing the effective transverse K in the demonstration?
questions.answer: K denotes restoring stiffness in the displayed motion direction. The transverse return depends on the pre-tension and geometry of the segments, rather than simply the axial spring constant considered in isolation. The demonstration explicitly matches the transverse restoring coefficient to the longitudinal one. Changing an axial property without establishing a larger restoring effect across the spring line does not establish the same frequency prediction.
rubric: Identify K as effective stiffness in the motion direction.
Distinguish changing axial spring constant from establishing a larger transverse restoring effect.

questions.prompt: An animation frame catches all the masses on their equilibrium marks. What extra observation would distinguish an instant of zero displacement from a displacement node?
questions.answer: Follow the same location through the motion. A moving mass can cross equilibrium for an instant and then continue to the other side. A displacement node in a pure mode remains at equilibrium throughout that mode’s oscillation. One frame cannot establish that persistent condition.
rubric: Distinguish momentary zero displacement from persistent zero displacement.
Require observing the same location across phases of the specified mode.
questions.topic: A node versus an equilibrium crossing

questions.prompt: In the three-mass comparison, describe the relationship among the outer masses and the middle mass in the lowest and highest modes. Why does counting the physical masses not distinguish those two rows?
questions.answer: The same three masses appear in both rows. In the lowest mode they move together, with the middle mass making the largest excursion. In the highest mode the outer masses move together while the middle mass moves oppositely. The changing relative pattern alters the deformation of their couplings, so a different coordinated pattern and rate can occur without adding or removing masses.
rubric: Describe together-motion in the lowest mode and middle-versus-ends opposition in the highest.
Keep the physical system fixed while attributing the difference to coordinated pattern.
questions.topic: Comparing the first and third modes

questions.prompt: How would you use several phases of these ideal undamped animations to check whether a mode is fading, rather than judging from one nearly flat frame?
questions.answer: Compare the largest excursions reached in successive cycles of the same mode. A nearly flat frame can be an equilibrium crossing within an oscillation that later returns to its full excursion. The source models undamped motion, so the excursion should not progressively shrink from cycle to cycle. Looking across phases separates that recurring crossing from a fading amplitude.
rubric: Compare successive cycle maxima instead of one frame.
Connect the undamped assumption to continuing excursion without progressive decay.

questions.prompt: The atlas has an empty cell in the three-mass row under mode 5. Explain the empty cell and the physical information carried by a row, without treating the blank as a missing video.
questions.answer: A row specifies how many masses can move in the displayed direction. Three moving masses provide three independent modes, so modes 4 and 5 do not belong in that row. Rows with more moving masses have more available patterns, producing the triangular layout. The blank indicates a pattern outside that system’s mode count rather than an unplayed phase.
rubric: Read row labels as moving-mass count.
Explain the triangular layout using the available mode count in each row.

questions.prompt: The atlas scales each pattern to the same maximum displayed displacement. What comparison is this choice useful for, and what amplitude comparison would it make misleading?
questions.answer: The shared visual scale helps compare where masses move together or oppositely and where reversals occur along a row. It does not show the naturally excited amplitude of one mode relative to another, because those displayed maxima were deliberately matched. A taller-looking local part must be interpreted within the scaled pattern rather than as evidence that its physical mode was excited more strongly.
rubric: Identify spatial-pattern comparison as the purpose of normalization.
Avoid inferring relative natural excitation from matched displayed maxima.

questions.prompt: The five fixed–fixed rows have different numbers of lobes, yet the supports do not change. Explain how higher modes can differ internally while satisfying the same endpoint requirement.
questions.answer: Both endpoints stay at zero displacement in every row. Higher modes fit additional alternating half-waves between those same supports, introducing internal locations of zero displacement and regions moving oppositely. The interior pattern can therefore become more complex while preserving the fixed ends. Under the ideal string conditions, those shorter spatial patterns have higher frequencies.
rubric: Keep both endpoint displacements zero for every mode.
Connect additional internal half-waves and reversals with a higher mode under the same boundary conditions.

questions.prompt: Design a comparison that isolates the effect of freeing one endpoint. Which conditions should remain matched, and which feature of the result should be measured?
questions.answer: Use the same ideal string length and wave speed, changing the endpoint condition from fixed to free while retaining the other fixed end. Measure the fundamental frequency in each condition rather than retuning both examples to the same displayed frequency. Under those matched conditions, the fixed–free fundamental is half the fixed–fixed fundamental. Separate retuning would obscure the boundary effect.
rubric: Hold length and wave speed fixed while changing one endpoint.
Measure the fundamental and distinguish the matched comparison from separately retuned illustrations.

questions.prompt: The combined string is labeled “Same string, all at once.” Explain how the separate mode panels determine one spatial displacement pattern, rather than representing five independent physical strings.
questions.answer: The panels isolate five possible contributions to the motion of the same string. At each position and instant, their signed displacements are added to obtain the displacement of that point in the combined field. Different positions receive different combinations because each mode has its own spatial shape. The bottom panel is therefore one changing string shape formed by superposition, not five strings occupying separate copies of the space.
rubric: Interpret the separate panels as contributions to one physical string.
Explain addition of signed displacement at each position and instant to form the full field.
questions.topic: Constructing one spatial field from modes

questions.prompt: Why do the 100–500 Hz frequency labels remain meaningful when the string motion is shown at one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of its physical speed?
questions.answer: The labels identify the intended physical frequencies. The animation slows the time course uniformly so the motions can be inspected. All modes undergo the same time scaling, preserving their relative rates and the harmonic relationship. A cycle counted directly in playback time is a slowed display cycle, not a 100 Hz physical cycle occurring at normal speed.
rubric: Separate physical frequency labels from playback time.
Explain that uniform slowing preserves relative rates and harmonic relationships.

questions.prompt: Why does the black pickup point matter when connecting the combined string drawing to its amplitude spectrum?
questions.answer: The spectrum reports the motion measured at that location rather than a spatial average of the whole string. Each mode contributes according to how much that point moves in the mode. The source chooses modal amplitudes so the five contributions have equal measured heights there. The full string drawing supplies spatial information that the single-point spectrum alone does not display.
rubric: Identify the spectrum as a measurement at the marked location.
Distinguish local modal contributions from the full spatial field.
questions.topic: A local measurement of a spatial system

questions.prompt: The membrane patterns are labeled (2,1) and (1,2). What difference do those ordered pairs encode, and why should they not be read as two lists of spectral peak frequencies?
questions.answer: The pair counts half-wave divisions in the membrane’s two spatial directions. The (2,1) pattern divides twice along the first direction and once along the other, while (1,2) exchanges those roles. The numbers describe shape, not frequencies in Hz. The illustration assigns the displayed frequencies separately, and its natural eigenfrequencies should not be inferred from those pair labels alone.
rubric: Interpret the two entries as divisions along two spatial directions.
Separate spatial mode labels from assigned frequency labels.

questions.prompt: The combined membrane panel looks vertically flatter than an individual-mode panel. Why would that picture alone be a poor test of whether adding the modes weakened the motion?
questions.answer: The combined surface is displayed at a reduced vertical scale so it fits in its panel. Its apparent height therefore cannot be compared directly with the magnified individual panels. The physical mixture is the sum of their contributions, while the drawing’s scale is a separate representational choice. Compare values or drawings on a shared scale before inferring weaker motion.
rubric: Identify the deliberate reduced vertical scale of the combined panel.
Separate display magnification from the summed displacement being represented.

questions.prompt: At one marked mass and one instant, the two contributing modes have equal displacements in opposite directions. Explain why zero displacement in their sum at that instant does not mean either mode has been removed.
questions.answer: The simultaneous contributions cancel at that mass at that instant. Each mode continues to oscillate at its own rate, so their relative contributions can change afterward and cancellation can disappear. A temporary zero in the sum is different from deleting a component or establishing a persistent node of the whole motion.
rubric: Apply addition to the simultaneous opposite displacements.
Keep temporary local cancellation distinct from removing a mode or making a permanent node.

questions.prompt: Suppose a carefully measured laryngeal signal has nearly equally spaced peaks. Explain what this would support and what it would leave unsettled about the membrane model.
questions.answer: The hypothetical measurement would support the specific predicted regular spacing for that signal under those recording conditions. It would not by itself establish that the model explains every feature of vocal-fold motion, nor that every membrane’s natural eigenfrequencies are harmonic. The source’s illustrative membrane frequencies are assigned, so agreement with one prediction must remain distinct from a universal proof. The lecture page itself supplies no completed participant result.
rubric: Treat the stated observation as hypothetical evidence for the particular spacing prediction.
Avoid extending one agreement into universal membrane or complete-model proof.
questions.topic: What agreement with a prediction establishes

questions.prompt: Two hypothetical spectra have peaks at the same regularly spaced frequencies but different peak heights. Would that difference alone decide against the lecture’s equal-spacing prediction? Explain the measurement that matters.
questions.answer: No. The prediction concerns gaps between the peak frequencies, not equality of their amplitudes. Compare the horizontal frequency positions and their successive gaps in each spectrum. Different heights can leave those gaps unchanged. Equal-height schematic peaks illustrate a chosen amplitude setup and are not a requirement of the stated laryngeal spacing test.
rubric: Identify frequency gaps as the predicted quantity.
Separate variable peak amplitudes from a violation of equal frequency spacing.

questions.prompt: The separately tuned string illustrations both start at 100 Hz. Describe a feature of their higher-frequency spectra that still distinguishes the fixed–fixed from the fixed–free example.
questions.answer: The fixed–fixed illustration includes consecutive multiples, with peaks at 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz. The fixed–free illustration includes the odd multiples shown at 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. Thus a common lowest frequency does not make their higher allowed patterns identical. The difference follows from having matching versus different endpoint conditions in the two ideal systems.
rubric: Compare consecutive with odd-multiple spectral components.
Relate that distinction to endpoint conditions despite the matched displayed fundamental.

questions.prompt: In the three-row comparison, the heavier transverse mass makes fewer cycles than the reference, while the stiffer transverse system makes more. Which interpretation uses the controls shown?

options.text: The comparison changes mass at matched K in one row and effective restoring stiffness at matched mass in the other, producing opposite rate changes.
options.feedback: The heavier mass slows the cycle under unchanged restoring stiffness, whereas the stronger restoring effect speeds it under unchanged mass.

options.text: The heavier row isolates a change in restoring stiffness, while the stiffer row isolates a change in inertia, because the drawing’s thickness supplies the mass label.
options.feedback: This exchanges the manipulated properties. The labels distinguish 4m with K from m with 4K.

options.text: The two changed rows isolate displacement amplitude, so their cycle counts should be interpreted as two different ways of drawing the same frequency.
options.feedback: The observed cycle-count changes concern frequency rather than merely amplitude.

options.text: The heavier and stiffer rows differ because one is transverse and the other longitudinal, making direction the uncontrolled cause of the different rates.
options.feedback: Both directions appear in each row. The comparison can be made within the transverse column while changing the stated mechanical property.

questions.answer: The heavier mass slows the cycle under unchanged restoring stiffness, whereas the stronger restoring effect speeds it under unchanged mass.
rubric: Identify what is held fixed in each row.
Connect the opposite rate changes with mass versus restoring stiffness.
questions.topic: Using the controls in the rate comparison

questions.prompt: A lab wants to reproduce the demonstration’s matched rates for longitudinal and transverse motion. Which plan makes a difference in direction interpretable without assuming that direction alone fixes the rate?

options.text: Match the masses but use any two available springs, then attribute a cycle-rate difference to longitudinal versus transverse motion without checking restoring action.
options.feedback: Unmatched effective restoring action can produce the rate difference independently of direction.

options.text: Match the largest visible excursion, then compare one image of each system as evidence that their cycle rates are equal.
options.feedback: Matched displacement size and one image do not establish a matched repetition rate.

options.text: Match moving mass and effective restoring stiffness in each displayed direction, then record displacements across enough time to compare cycle rates.
options.feedback: The source matches mass and effective restoring action across directions. Repeated displacement measurements establish rate rather than inferring it from orientation or one frame.

options.text: Match the axial spring constants and ignore pre-tension and geometry, treating those properties as irrelevant once the two masses have the same size.
options.feedback: The transverse restoring coefficient depends on pre-tension and geometry in this idealization.

questions.answer: The source matches mass and effective restoring action across directions. Repeated displacement measurements establish rate rather than inferring it from orientation or one frame.
rubric: Control mass and effective stiffness in the appropriate direction.
Measure repetition over time rather than static position.

questions.prompt: The longitudinal oscillator has total stiffness K. In the matched transverse illustration, each of the two pre-tensioned segments contributes K/2 in the transverse direction. What follows for the comparison?

options.text: The transverse total is K/2, since the mass can receive a restoring effect from the segment on the side toward which it is displaced.
options.feedback: Both pre-tensioned segments contribute to the effective transverse restoring effect in this model.

options.text: The transverse total is 2K, since two visible segments each replace the full longitudinal spring despite the K/2 contribution stated for each.
options.feedback: This counts each half contribution as a full K instead of combining the specified contributions.

options.text: The transverse contributions cancel because the endpoints lie on opposite sides, leaving no restoring action across the line.
options.feedback: Their horizontal orientations do not cancel the transverse restoring components that return the displaced mass toward equilibrium.

options.text: The two transverse contributions together match K, so counting two segments does not by itself imply twice the restoring stiffness of the longitudinal example.
options.feedback: The contributions are halves of the total matched stiffness. The source assigns them so the same mass has the same cycle rate in the two directions.

questions.answer: The contributions are halves of the total matched stiffness. The source assigns them so the same mass has the same cycle rate in the two directions.
rubric: Combine the stated transverse restoring contributions.
Keep segment count distinct from total effective stiffness.
questions.topic: Total restoring action from two segments

questions.prompt: Two displacement traces reach their maxima at different moments. Before calling them different-frequency modes, which additional observation would separate a phase difference from a rate difference?

options.text: Compare their vertical peak heights, treating a larger displacement excursion as evidence that its maxima repeat at a higher frequency.
options.feedback: Peak height measures amplitude, not the interval defining cycle rate.

options.text: Compare the intervals between repeated corresponding points on each trace, such as successive maxima, rather than comparing the timing of one peak.
options.feedback: Phase can shift when peaks occur without changing their repetition interval. Different frequencies require different cycle rates, as distinct from one offset in timing.

options.text: Compare whether the traces are positive at the same instant, treating opposite signs in one frame as enough to establish different frequencies.
options.feedback: Equal-frequency motions can have opposite signs because of phase. One instant does not establish their repetition rates.

options.text: Compare which trace reaches its first displayed maximum earlier, treating the initial timing offset as the length of the slower cycle.
options.feedback: The first displayed peak can depend on the starting phase, so its timing alone is not a cycle interval.

questions.answer: Phase can shift when peaks occur without changing their repetition interval. Different frequencies require different cycle rates, as distinct from one offset in timing.
rubric: Measure repeated-cycle intervals.
Distinguish a timing offset from a difference in repetition rate.
questions.topic: Phase versus frequency in a recording

questions.prompt: In the same-direction two-mass mode, both masses have equal displacement along the chain. Why can a restoring response remain even when their middle coupling keeps the same length?

options.text: The outer couplings deform as each mass moves relative to its fixed support, so constant middle separation does not eliminate restoring action.
options.feedback: Equal displacements preserve the separation of the masses, but each moves relative to its adjacent fixed support. The outer couplings still provide restoring contributions.

options.text: The unchanging middle coupling must supply the entire restoring response, because the outer couplings translate with the masses and lose contact with the supports.
options.feedback: The outer ends remain fixed. The outer couplings deform as the masses move relative to those supports.

options.text: The middle coupling keeps its length by preventing the masses from moving, making the visible displacement a shift of the equilibrium line rather than an oscillation.
options.feedback: The masses do move together relative to the fixed equilibrium marks. Fixed separation does not imply zero displacement.

options.text: The equal displacements remove deformation from all three couplings, so the repeated motion must be generated by an added external drive rather than restoring action.
options.feedback: Only the middle separation is unchanged in this pure pattern. The outer couplings still deform in the undamped model.

questions.answer: Equal displacements preserve the separation of the masses, but each moves relative to its adjacent fixed support. The outer couplings still provide restoring contributions.
rubric: Distinguish mass-to-mass separation from mass-to-support separation.
Identify the outer restoring contributions in the together mode.
questions.topic: Where restoring action comes from in together-motion

questions.prompt: A three-mass recording shows the middle mass away from equilibrium while the outer masses occupy opposite sides of their equilibrium positions. Which classification fits the displayed pure-mode patterns?

options.text: This identifies pure mode 2, since opposite outer positions are enough to classify it even when the middle mass has substantial displacement.
options.feedback: The nonzero middle displacement contradicts pure mode 2, whose middle mass remains at equilibrium.

options.text: This identifies pure mode 3, since its defining relationship is that the two outer masses oppose one another while the middle mass follows either one.
options.feedback: In mode 3 the two outer masses move together, with the middle mass opposing them.

options.text: It can be mixed motion, since the moving middle contradicts mode 2 and the opposite outer displacements contradict modes 1 and 3.
options.feedback: No one of the three depicted pure patterns has this combination. Adding mode contributions can produce a relationship not matching a pure-mode row.

options.text: This identifies pure mode 1, since being the lowest mode lets each mass move independently of the other two at the same instant.
options.feedback: Mode 1 has a coordinated together-motion pattern, not three independent displacement signs.

questions.answer: No one of the three depicted pure patterns has this combination. Adding mode contributions can produce a relationship not matching a pure-mode row.
rubric: Use the middle and outer relationships together.
Recognize that the given relationship differs from every depicted pure mode.
questions.topic: Diagnosing a mixture from spatial relationships

questions.prompt: Mode 1 appears in both the two-mass and six-mass rows of the atlas. What does the shared label establish when comparing those two systems?

options.text: It establishes the same absolute frequency because the first column fixes a rate shared by systems with different numbers of masses.
options.feedback: The column identifies mode order. Changing the chain’s size changes the physical system rather than preserving a column-defined rate.

options.text: It establishes the same number of displacement nodes because the first column requires the two chains to contain the same number of moving elements.
options.feedback: The rows have different moving-mass counts. A shared mode label does not equate those inventories.

options.text: It identifies two phases of one six-mass motion, with the two-mass row showing the other four masses at a moment of zero displacement.
options.feedback: The row labels denote different systems, not different phases with hidden masses.

options.text: It identifies each system’s first, lowest-frequency pattern, without establishing that their absolute frequencies are equal across different row sizes.
options.feedback: Mode number orders patterns within a specified system. Shared labeling across different chains does not impose the same numerical frequency.

questions.answer: Mode number orders patterns within a specified system. Shared labeling across different chains does not impose the same numerical frequency.
rubric: Interpret mode number within its own system.
Avoid inferring equal absolute frequency from a shared column label.

questions.prompt: Within a single six-mass atlas row, you move from a pattern with few spatial reversals to a pattern with more neighboring regions moving oppositely. Which qualitative change accompanies that move?

options.text: The moving mass count increases, so the apparent reversals come from replacing the six-mass row with a chain containing more elements.
options.feedback: The count changes between rows, not between mode columns of one row.

options.text: The mode frequency increases while the physical mass count and the fixed-end conditions remain the same for that row.
